# Supplementary Material {.unnumbered}

::: {#suppfig-depth}
![](figureS1.png)

Control-level HPV detection within matched sequencing-depth bins. For each population tier, the percentage of libraries reaching the control-calibrated detection floor (`r p1(stats$floor_rpm)` RPM) is plotted within five total-read bins (<5M, 5–10M, 10–20M, 20–40M, >40M reads); a tier is drawn in a bin only where it has at least three libraries. Productive controls (warts/condyloma) detect at 90–100% in every bin in which they occur, as do the EV biopsies and the peri-lesional mucosa in the deep bins where they fall, whereas cutaneous neoplasia (cSCC/actinic keratosis) and unselected skin stay near zero across all bins, including the deepest. This depth-matched comparison confirms that the tier difference in @fig-rpm is not produced by differences in sequencing depth: the tiers that reach the floor do so at every depth, and the tiers that do not never reach it, however deeply sequenced. Point size is proportional to the number of libraries in each tier × bin.
:::

::: {#supptbl-types}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cat(knitr::kable(build_type_table(), format = "pipe", align = c("l", rep("r", 6))), sep = "\n")
```

Number of libraries assigned to each HPV reference type across population tiers (types with ≥2 assigned libraries shown). Each cell also gives, in parentheses, the prevalence *within* that tier, the library count divided by the tier size in the column header, estimated as a Beta-Binomial posterior mean under a weakly-informative Beta(0.5, 0.5) prior. Because tier sizes span more than two orders of magnitude, raw counts are not comparable across tiers: the 14 HPV11 detections in productive controls and the 14 in peri-lesional mucosa correspond to very different prevalences (`r ciA("HPV11","control_productive")` versus `r ciA("HPV11","peri_lesional")`; posterior mean with 95% credible interval), and the high-risk mucosal types HPV16 and HPV18 are confined almost entirely to cell-line material (`r ciA("HPV16","cell_line")` and `r ciA("HPV18","cell_line")` of cell-line libraries, versus below 0.1% of skin libraries for both), the signature of integrated-HPV cell-line contamination. Productive controls are dominated by cutaneous wart and low-risk types (HPV57, HPV2, HPV27, HPV6/11, HPV42); the EV tier by the beta-types that define the syndrome (HPV9, HPV14, HPV20, HPV25, HPV47); peri-lesional mucosa by the mucosal alpha repertoire of the adjacent condylomata (HPV11, HPV42, HPV6, HPV74, HPV90). The neoplasia-associated infections are the gamma- and alpha-types HPV12, HPV16, HPV96 and HPV182. Unselected skin contributes no type above the two-library display threshold apart from two HPV18 contamination calls: its beta/gamma reservoir lies below the breadth-and-depth assignment criterion and appears instead in @supptbl-trace. @suppfig-genus summarises this table, and @supptbl-trace, at the level of HPV genus.
:::

::: {#supptbl-productive}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cat(knitr::kable(build_prod_table(), format = "pipe", align = c("l", "l", "l", "r", "r", "r")), sep = "\n")
```

Genuine, non-cell-line productive HPV infections detected in primary skin and skin-associated tissue. Each library met the productive criterion (≥3 L1 major-capsid reads) and was flagged as primary tissue rather than cell line or engineered material. Coverage breadth is the maximum across assigned references for that sample. In the two "other-tissue" co-infections (ERR2274877, ERR1971044) the co-infecting gamma-type HPV182 reached 98–99% genome coverage at 243–245× mean depth. These cases show that bona fide productive cutaneous beta- and gamma-HPV infection does occur in primary tissue, but against the population-scale null they are the exception (see main text and @fig-rpm).
:::

::: {#supptbl-bayes}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cat(knitr::kable(build_bayes_table(stats, bget), format = "pipe", align = c("l", "l", "l", "r")), sep = "\n")
```

Bayesian re-analysis of the principal contrasts under weakly-informative priors. Each frequentist model (M1–M3; Methods, @tbl-positivity, @fig-rpm) was refitted as a Bayesian logistic regression with a Normal(0, 2.5) prior on the log-odds coefficients and a Normal(0, 5) prior on the intercept (`rstanarm`; four chains, all R-hat ≤ 1.004, no divergent transitions). Odds ratios are posterior medians with 95% credible intervals; P(OR > 1) is the posterior probability of a positive effect. Frequentist odds ratios (with *P* values) are shown for comparison; the productive-controls-versus-skin row is a Fisher exact estimate inflated by near-complete separation, whose Bayesian counterpart is regularised by the prior (a heavier-tailed Student-*t*(3) prior gives an even larger posterior OR, `r bor(bget("M2c_controls_vs_skin_floor_studentt"))`, confirming robustness). Sequencing depth is modelled per 10-fold (log₁₀) change in library size.
:::

::: {#supptbl-cin}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cat(knitr::kable(cin_tbl, format = "pipe", align = c("l", "l", "l", "l", "l", "r")), sep = "\n")
```

High-risk mucosal HPV16 cases captured by the broadened cutaneous-neoplasia query and conservatively retained in the neoplasia tier. All `r stats$cin_n` are typed as the mucosal high-risk type HPV16 (dominant assigned reference) with cervical/CIN or unspecified-site diagnoses, and all exceed the control-calibrated detection floor (`r p1(stats$floor_rpm)` RPM), so they make up `r stats$cin_n` of the `r stats$neo_pos_floor` above-floor detections in the whole tier. Excluding them halves cutaneous-neoplasia floor-level detection, from `r pp(stats$neo_pctfloor)`% to `r pp(stats$neo_pctfloor_cut)`% (versus unselected skin: OR `r fo(stats$m2b_or_cut)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$m2b_p_cut)`, down from OR `r fo(stats$m2b_or)`), and strengthens the warts/EV-versus-neoplasia productivity contrast from OR `r fo(stats$m3_or)` to OR `r fo(stats$m3_or_cut)` (*P* = `r fp(stats$m3_p_cut)`). Retaining them is therefore the conservative analytical choice: the small floor-level excess of neoplasia over skin reported in the main text is an upper bound.
:::

::: {#supptbl-trace}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cat(knitr::kable(build_trace_table(), format = "pipe", align = c("l","l","r","r","r","r","r","r")), sep = "\n")
```

Detection-tier HPV type catalogue. This table is the complement of @supptbl-types, not an extension of it: it contains only the `r stats$trace_n` HPV-positive libraries that fell *below* the breadth ≥ 0.10 and depth ≥ 2 assignment threshold and therefore have no entry in @supptbl-types. A library appears in exactly one of the two tables. That is why tiers dominated by high-coverage infection are nearly empty here: of the `r stats$ctrl_n` productive-control libraries, `r stats$ctrl_n - trace_elig("control_productive")` are assigned a type in @supptbl-types and only `r trace_elig("control_productive")` remain eligible for this table, of which `r stats$trace_ctrl_resolved` resolve; the peri-lesional tier contributes none at all. The near-absence of productive controls from the detection tier is a positive control on the assignment criterion, not a missing signal. For each eligible library the best-hit reference was taken from unique STAR primary alignments (MAPQ 255); `r stats$trace_resolved` resolved to a confident low-coverage type spanning `r stats$trace_ntypes` types (those with ≥ 2 resolved calls shown), with genus from the complete PaVE lookup. These are low-coverage, non-productive detections: the type is confidently identified but genome coverage is below the assignment breadth, so they extend the descriptive type catalogue without bearing on productivity. As in @supptbl-types, each cell gives the count with its prevalence among *all* libraries of that tier in parentheses (Beta-Binomial posterior mean, Beta(0.5, 0.5) prior; tier sizes in the headers), keeping both tables on one denominator; the trace-eligible counts per tier are `r trace_elig_str()`. Healthy skin is dominated by cutaneous beta/gamma/nu types (`r stats$trace_skin_cut` of `r stats$trace_skin_n` resolved skin calls), whereas the mucosal types HPV16 and HPV18 concentrate in cell-line and other material (HPV16 trace prevalence `r ciT("HPV16","cell_line")` in cell lines versus `r ciT("HPV16","unselected_skin")` in skin), reproducing the contamination pattern of @supptbl-types at the sensitivity floor. @suppfig-genus collapses this table, and @supptbl-types, from HPV type to HPV genus.
:::

::: {#suppfig-genus}
![](figureS2.png)

HPV genus prevalence by population tier. The two type catalogues are collapsed from HPV type to HPV genus: the assigned-type catalogue of @supptbl-types (top row), the detection-tier trace catalogue of @supptbl-trace (middle row), and their union (bottom row), a library contributing to at most one of the first two rows. Points are Beta-Binomial posterior means with 95% credible intervals (Beta(0.5, 0.5) prior), computed exactly as in the two tables so that a cell here and the corresponding table cell quote the same prevalence; the number above each point is the count of libraries detected, and the denominator is the tier size (Methods). Grey crosses mark tiers in which a genus was never detected; they sit at the axis floor because the *y*-axis is log-scaled and the lowest tick, labelled 0, is a placeholder for zero. A library carrying two types of different genera contributes to both, so the points within a tier need not sum to that tier's positivity rate.

Read across the bottom row, the figure is the type landscape of the study in one panel. The productive controls are alpha-dominated (`r kG("Alpha","Productive controls")` libraries, `r ciG("Alpha","Productive controls")`) with a gamma minority (`r ciG("Gamma","Productive controls")`) and no beta at all, the repertoire of cutaneous and mucocutaneous warts. The EV biopsies are the mirror image, essentially pure beta (`r kG("Beta","EV")`, `r ciG("Beta","EV")`), which is the genus the syndrome is defined by. Peri-lesional mucosa is purely alpha (`r kG("Alpha","Peri-lesional mucosa")`), carrying its adjacent condylomata's types and nothing cutaneous. Cell lines are alpha (`r ciG("Alpha","Cell line")`), the integrated HPV16/HPV18 contamination signature. Against these, unselected skin is flat and low: alpha, beta and gamma occur at indistinguishable rates near `r ciG("Beta","Unselected skin")`, joined by the only nu detections in the study (`r kG("Nu","Unselected skin")` libraries, HPV41), the profile of a sparse commensal reservoir rather than of any one disease. Cutaneous neoplasia is the one tissue tier in which beta exceeds alpha (`r ciG("Beta","Neoplasia")` versus `r ciG("Alpha","Neoplasia")`), consistent with a beta-HPV footprint, though at prevalences one to two orders of magnitude below the productive tiers. The mu genus (HPV1, the classic plantar-wart type) was detected in no tier.
:::

::: {#supptbl-coinf}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cat(knitr::kable(build_coinf_table(), format = "pipe", align = c("l", "l", "l", "l")), sep = "\n")
```

Libraries carrying more than one assigned HPV type. Every library in which two or more references independently cleared the assignment criterion (coverage breadth ≥ 0.10 **and** mean depth ≥ 2) is listed, with each type's breadth and mean depth, ordered by depth. `r cf$libs` of the `r cf$typed` typed libraries qualify (`r cf$k2` with two types, `r cf$k3` with three, `r cf$k4` with four, `r cf$k5` with five). Coverage is computed by `samtools coverage -q 10`, which retains only uniquely-mapped reads, since STAR assigns MAPQ ≤ 3 to any read placing equally well on two references. Cross-mapping between similar types therefore cannot manufacture a co-infection call; each type in a row is supported by reads that map to it and to nothing else.

Three cautions govern how far this table can be read. First, **the rows are not independent observations**. `r cf$pair_libs` of the `r cf$libs` come from the paired studies SRP314958 (RNA-seq) and SRP314961 (MeRIP-seq), which are the same `r cf$pair_donors` donors, five condyloma lesions (CA_1 to CA_5) and four matched peri-lesional specimens (CON_1 to CON_4), each sequenced as an RNA-seq library plus a MeRIP input and IP fraction. Rows sharing a donor carry near-identical read profiles. Second, **the secondary types often sit close to the threshold**: across all non-dominant calls the median depth is `r p1(cf$sec_med_depth)`× and `r cf$sec_shallow`% fall below 5×, so which type is called second can depend on the library fraction. In donor CA_2 the RNA-seq and MeRIP input fractions call HPV6 + HPV11 while the IP fraction of the same specimen calls HPV6 + HPV42. Third, the dominant type in a co-infected library typically exceeds its partner by two to three orders of magnitude in depth, so most rows describe one established infection with a minor second type rather than two comparable ones.

Where both partners are unambiguous the pairings are biologically coherent. Two "other-tissue" carcinoma and actinic-keratosis libraries (ERR2274877, ERR1971044) carry the gamma-types HPV96 and HPV182 together at 98–99% breadth and 61–245× depth. An EV biopsy (SRR21205038) carries the beta-types HPV20 and HPV9 at 18,558× and 736×. Both are two full genomes in one library, not a genome plus a fragment.

The most frequent pairing in the study is HPV11 with HPV42: `r cf$both1142` libraries carry both, `r cf$only11` carry HPV11 without HPV42, and only `r cf$only42` carry HPV42 without HPV11. In the peri-lesional tier the association is forced by the marginals of @supptbl-types, where 14 HPV11 and 13 HPV42 calls are distributed over 15 libraries. Applying a stricter bar to both partners (breadth ≥ 0.70 and depth ≥ 5× for each) leaves `r cf$strict_libs` libraries from `r cf$strict_donors` donors: one condyloma lesion (CA_1) and two peri-lesional specimens (CON_1, CON_3).

The dominance relation between the two types is asymmetric, but not cleanly so. HPV11 is the deeper type in all five condyloma lesions, exceeding HPV42 48- to 4,100-fold in the three with a strong HPV11 signal (CA_1, CA_4, CA_5) and 2- to 4-fold in the other two. In peri-lesional mucosa the picture splits: in CON_1 and CON_3, the two specimens where HPV42 is unambiguous, HPV42 is the deeper type (955× versus 138×, and 3,816× versus 9×, i.e. 7-fold and 410-fold), whereas in CON_2, CON_4 and CON_5, where HPV42 barely clears the assignment threshold, HPV11 remains the deeper type. Whether this reflects a genuine tissue difference in which type predominates, or merely that HPV42 clears the threshold only where it happens to be abundant, cannot be settled from three donors of one study. It is a hypothesis the data motivate, not a result they support.
:::
